title: Incorporation of the Excessive Fines Clause
signal: A state or local government actor seeks a grossly disproportionate forfeiture for a minor violation; the defendant invokes the Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause through the Fourteenth Amendment; the government moves to dismiss on a federal-only theory.
student_move: Cut the procedural-due-process misdirection and the automatic-win overclaim on the answer text. Then use the Gold Key to kill the federal-only trap.
tiny_rule: The Excessive Fines Clause is incorporated against the states (and their political subdivisions) through the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause.
trap: Some Bill of Rights provisions were historically treated as federal-only; the Excessive Fines Clause is not one of them. Timbs v. Indiana (2019) squarely held that it is incorporated.

title: Negligent loss by a state actor is not a due process violation
signal: A due process claim under § 1983, sole allegation is a state employee's negligence, the loss is small property.
student_move: Cut the overclaim (every loss is a violation), the wrong-frame level of review (strict scrutiny), and the wrong-party trap (clerk's hearing). The negligence rule is the residual answer.
tiny_rule: Negligence is not a constitutional deprivation; the Due Process Clause targets deliberate or reckless state action.
trap: The overclaim that every property loss is a due process violation is the dominant trap; the proper remedy is a state tort claim, not § 1983.

title: Prior restraint — advance approval orders and red-herring doctrines
signal: A government court order entered before trial in a defamation case requires a private speaker to obtain advance approval from a government official (or a private party under a government order) before publishing any future speech about that official.
student_move: Apply the Gold Key: any advance-approval requirement imposed by a government order is a prior restraint. Do not be lured by red-herring facts (medium, ad revenue) toward the commercial-speech or 'not the institutional press' doctrines. Apply Silver Key #1 to cut the commercial-speech answer. Apply Silver Key #2 to cut the 'not the institutional press' answer.
tiny_rule: A court order requiring advance approval for speech is a prior restraint, regardless of medium or revenue model.
trap: The dominant trap is the commercial-speech answer (the ad-revenue fact is salient). The secondary trap is the 'not the institutional press' answer (the medium is salient). The weakest trap is the rational-basis answer (level-of-scrutiny mismatch).

title: Rational basis with bite — animus toward a group
signal: Government actor denies a routine permit; animus on the face of the hearing record; no legitimate interest articulated.
student_move: Cut tiered-absolute and colloquialism answers. Apply the Gold Key: animus is not a legitimate interest; the discriminator can lose at rational basis without strict scrutiny being triggered.
tiny_rule: Animus toward a group is not a legitimate government interest, even under rational basis review.
trap: Reaching for a tier-escalation argument (strict scrutiny) that does not exist.

title: Channels-of-commerce power — the channels, not the goods
signal: A federal statute targets the act of shipping stolen property across state lines; the defendant argues the in-state taking is outside federal reach.
student_move: Identify the regulated act (the use of a channel), then apply the channels-of-commerce power. The in-state origin of the taking is not a defense.
tiny_rule: The channels-of-commerce power reaches the channels themselves; the inquiry is whether the statute regulates the use of a channel, not whether the goods are commercially clean.
trap: The 'stolen goods are outside commerce' overreach (D) feels right because stolen goods have a dirty chain of title. The channels power is about the channel, not the goods.

title: Right to interstate travel and durational-residency rules
signal: A state durational-residency classification disadvantages new residents in a public benefit (welfare, Medicaid, food assistance, in-state tuition, voting, bar admission).
student_move: Apply the right-to-travel doctrine: the right to be treated equally to other residents once the traveler has established residence is a fundamental right. Durational-residency rules that burden that right trigger strict scrutiny.
tiny_rule: Public-benefit rules can still burden fundamental rights; durational-residency rules that disadvantage new residents trigger strict scrutiny.
trap: The 'public benefits are always discretionary' framing is the dominant trap; the right to travel is a fundamental right, and the discretionary-benefits reasoning collapses when the eligibility rule operates as a penalty on the exercise of a constitutional right.

title: State-action threshold in Equal Protection challenges to private actors
signal: A constitutional claim (Equal Protection or Due Process) is filed against a private actor with no government funding or public-function role.
student_move: Run the state-action threshold first. The Equal Protection Clause is, by its terms, a constraint on government action. The scrutiny tier is reached only after state action is established.
tiny_rule: The threshold problem is state action; the scrutiny tier is reached only after state action is established.
trap: The strict-scrutiny framing is the dominant trap; the student skips the threshold problem and goes straight to the scrutiny tier. The 'Constitution bans all private discrimination' overclaim and the 'rational-basis-deference' framing are also wrong levels of analysis.

title: Article IV P&I person-class threshold
signal: A non-natural-person entity (corporation, LLC, partnership) sues under only Article IV Privileges and Immunities.
student_move: Cut the merits. The clause's text and case law require a natural-person citizen of another state; a corporation is not a citizen. The case is resolved at the threshold.
tiny_rule: Article IV P&I protects only natural-person citizens of other states.
trap: The student bridges from 'interstate burden' to 'Article IV applies' or jumps to a 'fundamental burden' merits theory. Both miss the person-class threshold.

title: Tax-power frame before scrutiny frame
signal: Federal excise tax + revenue purpose + answer choices invoking strict scrutiny or equal protection.
student_move: Ask whether the stem gives a protected trigger. If not, stay in the revenue-tax frame.
tiny_rule: Bad economic effects do not by themselves invalidate a facial revenue tax.
trap: Picking the dramatic constitutional standard instead of the tax-power answer.

title: Tier trigger before tier label
signal: Answer names strict or intermediate scrutiny.
student_move: Ask what trigger the answer supplies.
tiny_rule: No valid trigger means default rational basis.
trap: Picking the strongest-sounding tier because the facts feel unfair.

title: Hidden grant terms
signal: Federal money plus states plus later undisclosed condition.
student_move: Ask whether the state could know the condition before accepting.
tiny_rule: No clear notice, no knowing acceptance.
trap: Treating federal spending as a blank check.

title: Neutral aid / secular-use restriction
signal: Religious and secular schools get the same educational aid, and the statute limits use to secular instruction.
student_move: Do not make religious-school aid per se unconstitutional. Look for neutrality and use restriction.
tiny_rule: Neutral + secular-use school aid usually defeats the per se Establishment Clause trap.
trap: Public money plus religious school feels automatically invalid.

title: Presidential subpoena = calibrated review
signal: Congress seeks President's personal information from a third party.
student_move: Cut automatic extremes; then apply the Gold Key.
tiny_rule: No automatic enforcement, no automatic immunity; court checks purpose, tailoring, and burdens.
trap: Choosing the branch slogan instead of the court's task.

title: Belief lane vs conduct lane
signal: A religion question says the state punishes holding, teaching, professing, or affirming a belief.
student_move: Cut answers that switch to conduct, churches only, or a different Religion Clause.
tiny_rule: Belief as such is protected; conduct is separate.
trap: The state justifies a belief ban by pointing to regulable conduct.

title: Classification First, Scrutiny Second
signal: Answer choices jump to strict scrutiny, rights in every context, or automatic discrimination.
student_move: Name the line the law draws before choosing a tier.
trap: Policy-disagreement and same-medication facts are not automatic scrutiny triggers.

title: Federal contractor: practical interference axis
signal: state regulation of a private federal contractor
student_move: Ask whether the state rule burdens the federal job.

title: Taxpayer Standing: Narrow Door, Not Open Gate
student_move: Cut 'any taxpayer' overclaims, then check the narrow spending-power/Establishment trigger.
tiny_rule: General no standing; Flast exception for congressional spending plus Establishment Clause.
trap: Treating all taxpayer challenges as allowed, or treating merits proof as standing proof.

title: Close-family household ≠ ordinary zoning
signal: A city rule excludes one close relative from a shared household.
student_move: Treat it as family-integrity due process after cutting wrong constitutional homes.
tiny_rule: Family household first; zoning only after the family trigger is absent.
trap: Treating every occupancy ordinance as ordinary rational-basis zoning.

title: Price Gate Across State Lines
signal: Sell here only if prices elsewhere satisfy this state’s rule.
student_move: Follow the price lever across the border.
tiny_rule: In-state access tied to out-of-state prices points to DCC extraterritorial price control.
